evidence.questionPrompt: 1. {{1}}: Smallpox has been completely eradicated thanks to vaccination.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The History of Vaccination
evidence.sourceExcerpt: Vaccination is one of the most effective public health interventions in human history. Before its development, infectious diseases including smallpox, polio, measles, and diphtheria killed or disabled millions of people annually and were considered inescapable facts of life. Today, smallpox has been completely eradicated, polio survives in only a handful of countries, and childhood diseases that once swept through populations in devastating waves are largely preventable with a single injection. Protection operates at both individual and population levels. When enough people are immune, an infected person has fewer opportunities to pass a pathogen onward, indirectly protecting people who cannot receive a particular vaccine. Sustaining that barrier requires broad coverage because local gaps can still permit outbreaks.

evidence.questionPrompt: 2. {{2}}: Variolation was first practised in the Ottoman Empire before spreading to China.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The History of Vaccination
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The foundational insight of vaccination—that exposure to a mild or weakened form of a disease could confer protection against the severe form—was not the product of a single discovery but emerged from centuries of observation. In China, practitioners of variolation were inoculating people against smallpox as early as the sixteenth century by introducing dried scabs from mild cases into healthy individuals through the nose or skin. The practice spread through the Ottoman Empire and reached England in the early eighteenth century, where it was championed by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had observed it in Constantinople. Variolation carried a small but real mortality risk—approximately two percent of those inoculated died—but this was far lower than the thirty percent case fatality rate of naturally acquired smallpox. Recipients could also transmit infection while recovering, so the practice remained dangerous to both the individual and the surrounding community. Its adoption nevertheless showed that people were prepared to accept a controlled risk to avoid a much greater one.
evidence.rationale: The cited passage contradicts the proposition or states the inverse with the relevant scope; the negative judgement is required.

evidence.questionPrompt: 8. Jenner (1796): Coined the word "{{8}}" from the Latin word for cow.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The History of Vaccination
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The decisive advance came in 1796, when English country physician Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had contracted cowpox—a mild disease transmitted from cows—seemed to be protected against smallpox. Testing this hypothesis on a young boy named James Phipps, Jenner inoculated him with cowpox material and subsequently exposed him to smallpox. Phipps did not develop the disease. Jenner published his findings in 1798, coining the term "vaccine" from the Latin word vacca (cow). His discovery was remarkable not because it was immediately understood—the germ theory of disease would not emerge for another century—but because it worked.

evidence.questionPrompt: 9. Pasteur: Developed vaccines against cholera, {{9}}, and rabies.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 1: The History of Vaccination
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries saw rapid expansion of vaccine development, driven by advances in bacteriology and virology pioneered by Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch. Pasteur developed vaccines against chicken cholera, anthrax, and rabies; Koch established the methodological framework for identifying disease-causing microorganisms. Once particular microbes could be linked to particular diseases, researchers could design and test preventive preparations more systematically. Production still required reliable methods for weakening or inactivating an organism, preserving the product, and ensuring that one batch behaved like the next. The introduction of vaccines against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis in the 1920s and 1930s dramatically reduced childhood mortality in industrialised countries.

evidence.questionPrompt: What does the passage say about the Luddites?
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 3: The Future of Work
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The fear that technological change will destroy jobs on a net basis has a long history. The Luddites—English textile workers who destroyed machinery in the early nineteenth century—feared, correctly, that mechanisation would eliminate their specific occupations. They were wrong, however, about the broader consequences: industrialisation ultimately created far more employment than it destroyed, raising living standards across the economy. That distinction between a task, an occupation, and total employment is central to the modern debate. Technology can remove one activity from a job while leaving other duties intact, or eliminate a local occupation while creating different work elsewhere. Aggregate gains do not guarantee that displaced individuals can move easily into the new roles. Economists who draw comfort from this history argue that technological change is fundamentally labour-complementing—creating new tasks, new industries, and new forms of work that offset the jobs displaced. Sceptics counter that artificial intelligence differs qualitatively from previous technologies because it can replicate not just manual labour but cognitive work, threatening a much broader range of occupations simultaneously.

evidence.questionPrompt: What does the "hourglass economy" described by Autor et al. refer to?
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 3: The Future of Work
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The empirical evidence so far is mixed. Routine cognitive and manual tasks—those that can be reduced to a set of predictable steps—have been automated at substantial rates since the 1980s. Jobs involving non-routine physical tasks (plumbing, surgery, hairdressing) and non-routine cognitive tasks (creative problem-solving, social intelligence, strategic judgement) have proved considerably more resilient. Studies by economists David Autor and colleagues have documented a polarisation of labour markets in advanced economies: middle-skill jobs in routine occupations have hollowed out, while demand has grown at both the high-skill and low-skill ends of the distribution. Growth at both ends does not imply equal rewards. High-skill work may command rising salaries, while many low-skill service roles remain poorly paid and offer limited progression. The result is an "hourglass economy" in which middle-income earners face declining opportunity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 3: The Future of Work
evidence.sourceExcerpt: Education systems face enormous pressure to adapt. Curricula designed for the industrial era, emphasising memorisation and standardised assessment, are increasingly misaligned with the cognitive competencies—adaptability, complex communication, creative thinking—that labour markets are beginning to demand. Educational reformers argue that learning to learn—developing the metacognitive skills to acquire and deploy new capabilities throughout a working life—is more valuable than mastery of any fixed body of knowledge. Updating skills cannot be confined to the years before a person enters employment if technology continues to change during a career. Employers, training institutions, and governments therefore face questions about who should fund repeated learning and how workers can study without losing their income. evidence.questionPrompt: 36. {{36}}: The ultimate effect of technological change on employment is presented as uncertain.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 3: The Future of Work
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The fear that technological change will destroy jobs on a net basis has a long history. The Luddites—English textile workers who destroyed machinery in the early nineteenth century—feared, correctly, that mechanisation would eliminate their specific occupations. They were wrong, however, about the broader consequences: industrialisation ultimately created far more employment than it destroyed, raising living standards across the economy. That distinction between a task, an occupation, and total employment is central to the modern debate. Technology can remove one activity from a job while leaving other duties intact, or eliminate a local occupation while creating different work elsewhere. Aggregate gains do not guarantee that displaced individuals can move easily into the new roles. Economists who draw comfort from this history argue that technological change is fundamentally labour-complementing—creating new tasks, new industries, and new forms of work that offset the jobs displaced. Sceptics counter that artificial intelligence differs qualitatively from previous technologies because it can replicate not just manual labour but cognitive work, threatening a much broader range of occupations simultaneously.

evidence.questionPrompt: 37. Jobs involving {{37}} problem-solving and social intelligence have proved more resilient to automation.
evidence.sourceTitle: Reading — Passage 3: The Future of Work
evidence.sourceExcerpt: The empirical evidence so far is mixed. Routine cognitive and manual tasks—those that can be reduced to a set of predictable steps—have been automated at substantial rates since the 1980s. Jobs involving non-routine physical tasks (plumbing, surgery, hairdressing) and non-routine cognitive tasks (creative problem-solving, social intelligence, strategic judgement) have proved considerably more resilient. Studies by economists David Autor and colleagues have documented a polarisation of labour markets in advanced economies: middle-skill jobs in routine occupations have hollowed out, while demand has grown at both the high-skill and low-skill ends of the distribution. Growth at both ends does not imply equal rewards. High-skill work may command rising salaries, while many low-skill service roles remain poorly paid and offer limited progression. The result is an "hourglass economy" in which middle-income earners face declining opportunity.
